prompt: For a finite set $V$, which conditions are necessary and sufficient for $R\subseteq V\times V$ to represent simple undirected adjacency, using both ordered pairs for each edge?

answers.explanation: Symmetry makes adjacency undirected, and irreflexivity excludes loops. A set of pairs cannot encode parallel copies of an edge.
Reflexivity adds a loop at every vertex.
Asymmetry forbids the reverse pairs required for undirected edges.
This permits only one direction between distinct vertices and requires loops.
A nonempty undirected edge would force loops under transitivity.
These define a strict partial order, not arbitrary undirected adjacency.
This is asymmetry, which excludes every undirected edge.
Missing at least one loop still allows loops at other vertices.
Connexity additionally forces every distinct pair to be adjacent, giving only complete graphs.
This additionally excludes triangles; a triangle is a valid simple undirected graph.
